title: The dignity of work
hook: his hometown neighbors know Jesus by one thing: his trade

segments.voice: Yesterday, Lazarus at the gate, and the preferential option for the poor. Your line was the poor first. Did one decision get a look from the other side of the gate? Day one thousand two hundred ninety-seven.

Who was Jesus to the people who grew up with him? In Mark, he comes home to Nazareth and teaches in the synagogue, and the neighbors can't get past one thing. In the Douay-Rheims: "Is not this the carpenter, the son of Mary?" The Greek word is tekton, a builder, a craftsman. Whatever the crowds had seen, his own town knew him by his trade, by hands that cut and fit and carried. Catholic teaching takes that seriously. In Christ, God worked with his hands. Today, the dignity of work.
screen: `HOME TO NAZARETH.` → `IS NOT THIS THE CARPENTER?` → `GOD WORKED WITH HIS HANDS.`

segments.voice: First, work isn't a punishment. In Genesis, before anything has gone wrong, the Douay-Rheims says: "the Lord God took man, and put him into the paradise of pleasure, to dress it, and to keep it." Work is there in paradise. What comes after the fall is the sweat and the thorns: work made hard, not work invented. Second, work is for the person, not the person for work. John Paul the Second wrote a whole letter on human work, and its center is this: the value of work comes first from the fact that the one doing it is a person. Scrubbing floors and running a company both carry the dignity of a human being at work. Nobody is only a cost on a spreadsheet. Third, workers have rights. Leo's Rerum Novarum told employers not to treat workers as things to make money from, and defended the right of workers to form their own associations. Later teaching names a just wage, safe conditions, and rest, which the Church treats as rights and not favors. Fourth, rest belongs to work. The same Genesis that gives the garden gives the seventh day, when God rests. The Catechism calls the sabbath a protest against slavery to work and the worship of money. A day off isn't laziness in this teaching. It's a reminder that a person is more than an output.
screen: `WORK BEFORE THE FALL.` · `WORK IS FOR THE PERSON.` · `WORKERS HAVE RIGHTS.` · then, large: `REST BELONGS TO WORK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: thank a worker. Settle, and breathe. Look at one thing near you, a chair, a cup, the clothes you're wearing, and let the hands behind it come into view. Someone built, grew, sewed, packed, drove, stocked. Most of them you'll never meet. Now pick one worker you will see today: a bus driver, a nurse, a mail carrier, a mechanic. Decide how you'll thank them, specifically, by name if you can. Not for being nice. For the work. If you pray, you can pray for them. The bell holds the time.
The dignity of work. In Catholic teaching, work is part of how people were made, it exists for the person, and workers have rights. Today's word.

Your line: work has dignity. Today, thank one worker for the work itself, and do one piece of your own work as if it mattered, because in this teaching it does. Day one thousand two hundred ninety-seven.

howItsDone: Catholics honor Saint Joseph the Worker with a feast day, some dioceses offer a Labor Day Mass, and Catholic teaching on just wages and workers' associations is cited in debates about labor.

notes: Tekton glossed as 'a builder, a craftsman' (standard lexicon sense: a worker in wood, stone or metal). Confirm.
Rerum Novarum paragraph numbers vary between editions; confirm 20 (workers not to be treated as chattels) and 48–51 (workers' associations).
Laborem Exercens 6 paraphrased: the basis for the value of work is that the one doing it is a person. 'A whole letter on human work' is a description, not a count.
CCC 2172 paraphrased: the sabbath as a protest against the servitude of work and the worship of money.
howItsDone mentions the feast of St. Joseph the Worker and a Labor Day Mass in some dioceses; confirm.
